I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Being superalert or watchful or on guard

I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'Being looked at sexually' is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision as the index trauma, especially when no other selected items suggest sexual trauma, harassment, or body-focused threat. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for signs that someone is entering the home implies an interpersonal intrusion/assault threat, which does not fit well with a motor vehicle collision and is not supported by the other items. The rest of the threat profile is general hypervigilance to sudden sounds, making this specific home-intruder monitoring item clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes usually implies clothing cues tied to the trauma context. For a motor vehicle collision, this is difficult to justify unless other items indicate clothing-specific trauma reminders, which they do not. It also does not connect plausibly to the selected triggers, which are taste, workplace, and sexual objectification.

Workplace as a trigger is weakly grounded for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision given the rest of the profile: the other trigger and threat items are sensory/accident-related, but nothing in appraisals, threat, or strategies explains why the workplace itself would be a salient trauma cue. This makes the trigger set less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste linked to a motor vehicle collision is possible but clinically unusual, and here it is unsupported by memory content or appraisals that would make a gustatory cue understandable. With no memory items and otherwise sound/crash/vehicle-focused content, this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, a specific taste trigger and an alcohol smell trigger are not impossible, but in combination they imply trauma details (e.g. ingestion, blood, alcohol involvement, hospital/chemical context) that are unsupported by the rest of the profile. The rest of the triggers, threat items, and appraisals are centered on vehicle crash/sound danger, so these sensory triggers look clinically disconnected from the trauma representation described elsewhere.

Undereating as a coping strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and avoidance-based coping around crash-related distress; avoid-driving and screen escape fit that pattern, but food restriction addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, memory, or appraisals. In this profile it appears clinically mismatched rather than a coherent extension of the same trauma-linked cycle.

vignette: The intersection on Route 9 had been clear until the delivery truck blew through the red light. Samir remembered the sickening crack of his sedan’s rear bumper, the violent spin across two lanes, and the deafening screech of twisting metal as he was pinned against the steering wheel. When firefighters finally cut him free, the air was thick with the sharp tang of spilled liquor from a nearby cab, and the wail of sirens echoed over the grinding of his own shattered engine. For weeks afterward, the memory did not fade; it returned in sudden, unbidden flashes. A glance at a parked sedan would instantly drag him back to the moment his own car folded like paper, while the faint whiff of bourbon from a passing driver’s cup would tighten his chest until he was certain another crash was inevitable. As the months passed, these intrusions quickly escalated into a permanent state of physical alarm. Every time the crash imagery surfaced or he caught the smell of alcohol in the air, his heart would hammer against his ribs and his shoulders would hike up instinctively. He was never truly at ease, his nervous system locked in a constant scan for danger. This heightened threat state meant that ordinary office doors slamming or distant car backfires made him jump as if struck, keeping his hypervigilance dialed to an exhausting maximum. What frightened him most was not the noise or the sights, but the realization that he felt fundamentally broken. He could not rely on himself to navigate a simple commute without his hands shaking, and he was certain he was no longer capable of doing the meticulous work that had defined his career as a tax inspector. Believing he would never again feel normal emotions, Samir began to withdraw. When the crash imagery grew too heavy, he would instinctively retreat to his phone, scrolling through games and endless feeds for hours to drown out the internal noise. He avoided eating because the act of sitting still felt unbearable, and he gave up driving entirely, taking a long detour on the bus just to avoid being anywhere near a steering wheel. This withdrawal only deepened his dread. The longer he sat isolated behind a screen and starved himself, the more he interpreted this paralysis as proof that he was permanently incapable and could no longer rely on himself. Convinced his emotions were permanently gone, he viewed the world through a lens of inherent danger, which in turn amplified his sense of threat every time a loud noise echoed through the hallway. Locked in this perpetual state of alarm, he found his attention irresistibly drawn to the very things he feared, his hyper-alert eyes locking onto matching car models and his nose catching alcohol on passersby, feeding the very intrusions he was trying to escape. His physical exhaustion and mental fatigue from screen addiction left his nerves raw, so ordinary sounds in the downtown tax office now felt like immediate threats. At his desk, the consequences were undeniable. A colleague’s dropped file made him startle violently, and the faint whiff of vanilla liqueur from the breakroom coffee pot sent him scrambling to the stairwell to catch his breath. His audits grew sloppy, missed deadlines piled up, and his supervisor began questioning his reliability after he failed to attend three consecutive client meetings because the thought of leaving his apartment paralyzed him. Divorced for two years and already isolated by the trauma, Samir found himself utterly alone with his unraveling routine. What finally brought him to the clinic was a panic attack during a routine audit review, triggered by the smell of a client’s mint liqueur and the distant thud of a falling folder. He sat on the floor of the supply closet, trembling, terrified that he had permanently lost the ability to function or feel joy again, and desperate for someone to show him how to stop waiting for the next crash.
